title: Unconditional exponential hardness of \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP
formal: Do there exist explicit positive constants c and \(\varepsilon\) such that no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm solves Euclidean \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP on n-dimensional rational lattices in time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\), for any fixed k, where N is the input bit length? The lower bound must be unconditional; deterministic and randomized classical algorithms are included among the algorithms ruled out.
why: Combines worst-case exponential hardness, a cryptographically relevant approximation gap and resistance to quantum computation in one unconditional theorem. A resolution would turn a central type of lattice-security assumption into a proved complexity bound and would go well beyond establishing \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
status_note: Full original formulation and model read; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution. Related reduction results were checked at abstract level and do not remove their hardness assumptions. Proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Bennett poses Open Problem 4.12 with explicit \(c,\varepsilon >0\) and approximation factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\), including quantum algorithms. It is distinct from the conditional polynomial-time hardness question immediately before it.

Lattice Problems Beyond Polynomial Time supplies quantitative worst-case-to-average-case reductions underlying the cryptographic motivation; its consequences depend on an appropriate lattice-hardness premise.

Hecht and Safra state deterministic-reduction hardness results for \(\ell p\) norms with \(p>2\) under complexity assumptions. Their abstract does not resolve the unconditional Euclidean quantum-time target.

sentences: The input is a rational basis for an n-dimensional lattice and a positive radius.
The task distinguishes a nonzero vector within that radius from the promise that every nonzero vector is farther away by a factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\).
The source asks for explicit \(c,\varepsilon >0\) and an unconditional lower bound excluding \(2^{cn}\)-time algorithms, up to polynomial input-processing factors.
The bound must also exclude randomized and quantum computation with bounded error.
Such a theorem would establish a powerful worst-case hardness foundation for lattice-based cryptography.

upgraded_from.title: Unconditional exponential hardness for cryptographic lattice problems

definitions: An instance is an invertible rational matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{n\times n}\) and a positive rational threshold r, all represented explicitly in binary with numerator, denominator, sign and delimiters included in N. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\). Its shortest nonzero Euclidean length is \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{(\sum i v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\); the minimum exists because B is invertible and the lattice is discrete. The promise problem \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP asks for YES when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})\le r\) and NO when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})>n^{1+\varepsilon}r\), promised that one holds. There is no correctness requirement in the gap between those cases. The same \(\varepsilon\) is used at every dimension. A bounded-error algorithm must give the correct answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised instance. Use a uniform quantum computation with a fixed finite universal gate set, such as Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements and classical control; qubits begin in the input state and zero auxiliary states, without advice, oracles or special quantum input access. Gate operations, classical control and input handling all count toward total worst-case running time, with the bound applying to every measurement branch. A single machine must work for all dimensions and bit lengths. The factor \(N^{k}\) explicitly accounts for the ordinary polynomial input-processing overhead suppressed in the source’s dimension-based exponential notation. Constants \(c,\varepsilon\) are chosen before the algorithm and may be specified as positive rational numbers, with their values part of a positive resolution; k and the hidden running-time constant may depend on the algorithm. The task is worst-case promise decision, not a claim about a supplied random distribution of bases.
answer_criterion: Specify positive constants \(c,\varepsilon\) and prove, without a complexity-theoretic or cryptographic hardness assumption, that no correct bounded-error quantum algorithm has running time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\) for any fixed k. Alternatively, refute the proposition by proving that for every \(c,\varepsilon >0\) there is an algorithm with such a running-time bound for some fixed k. Conditional hardness, exact-SVP hardness with approximation factor 1, and hardness in a different norm do not settle the stated target.

context_blocks.title: A large promise gap around the shortest vector
context_blocks.text: The input gives a lattice basis and a radius. A yes instance contains a nonzero lattice point within that radius; a no instance has every nonzero point farther away by a factor \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\). The question asks whether distinguishing these widely separated cases still requires exponential time in the dimension.

context_blocks.title: Why the approximation factor is essential
context_blocks.text: As the gap factor increases, fewer inputs satisfy the promise and the decision task can become easier. A lower bound for exact shortest vectors therefore does not establish hardness for the polynomially growing gap used here. Bennett’s Problem 4.12 combines a large approximation factor with an exponential lower bound.

context_blocks.title: Cryptographic significance
context_blocks.text: The STOC 2023 work connects exponential hardness of worst-case approximate lattice problems to average-case problems used for cryptography. Its abstract states that hardness at an approximately linear factor, up to logarithmic factors, would imply public-key cryptography. The survey’\(s n^{1+\varepsilon}\) target is chosen in this regime; the card itself asks for a concrete worst-case theorem.

context_blocks.title: Unconditional includes the quantum case
context_blocks.text: The desired result would establish a lower bound without assuming another problem is hard. It would also rule out bounded-error quantum algorithms. A 2025 result called deterministic hardness in other norms still assumes hardness of SAT-related problems; deterministic reductions and unconditional lower bounds are distinct notions.
